reason:
The artifact ships no test.py/get_inputs (files = kernel.py, meta.json, problem.txt), so problem.txt is the operative contract. It requires out[j] = scores[j] only when scores[j] is among the k largest and out[j] = 0 otherwise, and it limits the tie licence strictly to entries that "share the value at the k-th position". Claim c2 is confirmed, in_scope, and its scope evidence cites that contract text plus the kernel's fixed 40-step absolute-range bisection (kernel.py:15-21), which only guarantees lo <= v.

Decisive runtime evidence (t10, c2.e1): fp32 row [1e6] + 20 values clustered near 1e-3 spaced 1e-9, k=5 — the kernel kept all 21 entries, 16 of them strictly below the true k-th largest (1.0000159e-3, only 1 exact tie), with survivors down to 1.0000000e-3. These extras are not ties, are of the same magnitude as the legitimately selected cluster values, and therefore materially change the renormalized sampling weights the problem says are computed downstream. Follow-up t15 reproduces the same failure on a plainly in-domain distribution: peaked-softmax probability rows (64x512, T=0.1, k=50) violated in 64/64 rows with 17,878 kept entries strictly below the k-th largest and kept counts up to 427 instead of 50.

This is not a deviation the contract accounts for: the tie ambiguity clause covers only exact equality at the cutoff, no low-precision format is declared, and the failure is a wrong discrete selection set (and wrong nonzero outputs), not a reduction-order or rounding artifact. c1 (bisection stall on ±inf endpoints, kernel returns the input unchanged) is also confirmed but scoped "unknown" because problem.txt does not explicitly require non-finite inputs; I treat it as a corroborating generalization note, not the basis of the verdict. c3 (fp16/bf16 grid and overflow) was rebutted by t11 and is set aside. Note that benign cases (randn logits, T=1 softmax, T=0.03 softmax, 1e5-outlier logits) all passed exactly, so a naive random-input harness would miss this; the confirmed in-scope failures still stand.
